final_answer:
Short answer: only one office should indict, and it should be the office that can lay venue for the doctor's whole course of conduct in a single indictment, so that all the false claims in both states are charged together and sentenced together. The facts given do not say which district that is. On the stated facts (practice-related false claims in both states), the better-supported choice is the district where the larger share of the charged claims, and the scheme's center of gravity (billing, submission, or insurer processing), sits. Without those facts I cannot name one office with certainty.

Reasoning.
1. Venue limits the choice. Each count of 18 U.S.C. 1347 must be tried where the offense was committed (U.S. Const. art. III, sec. 2, cl. 3; amend. VI; Fed. R. Crim. P. 18). Under 18 U.S.C. 3237(a), an offense begun in one district and completed in another, or committed in more than one, may be prosecuted in any district in which it was begun, continued, or completed. So a single indictment can cover both states only if each count has a venue hook in the chosen district (for example, claims submitted from, processed in, or paid from there, or a single scheme with acts in that district). Claims made purely in the other state, with no connection to the chosen district, cannot be tried there. I could not retrieve the statutory text during research (egress blocked), so this rests on my knowledge of 3237(a).
2. Why one indictment beats two for maximum prison time under the Guidelines. (a) Loss is aggregated. Under USSG 2B1.1 loss drives the offense level, and under 1B1.3(a)(2) (relevant conduct, same course of conduct or common scheme) and the grouping rule 3D1.2(d), fraud counts group and loss from all the claims in both states is added together. A single sentencing therefore counts the full loss and gets the highest guideline range. (b) Statutory maximum and stacking. Section 1347 carries up to 10 years per count (20 if serious bodily injury, life if death). If the guideline range exceeds the statutory maximum on a single count, USSG 5G1.2(d) requires consecutive sentences on multiple counts to the extent needed to reach the total punishment. A single multi-count indictment lets the court stack counts to reach a guideline range above 10 years. (c) Separate prosecutions risk concurrency. If the second-sentencing district follows USSG 5G1.3, then where the first sentence arose from offenses that were fully taken into account in setting the second offense level (relevant conduct), the second sentence must run concurrently with an adjustment under 5G1.3(b); the Guidelines otherwise leave concurrent or consecutive to discretion (5G1.3(d)). Because the loss in each state would likely be counted as relevant conduct in the other case, the second prosecution adds little or no time and the doctor serves roughly the longest of the two sentences. Two separate cases also split loss, so each case might have a lower offense level than the combined one, and each would be capped at the 10-year per-count maximum without stacking across districts.
3. Other enhancers apply either way (2B1.1(b)(7) federal health care offense loss over $1 million; 3B1.3 abuse of position of trust), so they do not decide the choice.
4. Practical conclusion. The office that should indict is whichever has proper venue over all claims: choose the district where the scheme was centered or where the claims were processed, and that has the larger charged loss. If the prosecutors cannot establish venue in either district for the other state's claims, then the two offices should coordinate, with one filing first and the other seeking a Guidelines-consistent consecutive sentence under 5G1.3(d) (discretionary), recognizing that 5G1.3(b) would likely require concurrency. Note also that the question speaks of the 'District Court of South Carolina'; the proper entity is the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of South Carolina, and Georgia has three districts, so the Southern District only matters if the practice or claims touch it.

Caveats: the prompt provides no facts on where claims were submitted or the dollar amounts in each state, so the answer is conditional. I did not verify case law on 1347 venue or on 5G1.3 and 5G1.2(d) application during research.

claims.text: A single indictment in one district covering both states' claims maximizes time because loss aggregates and counts can be stacked under 5G1.2(d).
Separate prosecutions risk concurrent sentences under 5G1.3(b) because the other state's conduct is relevant conduct.
Single indictment requires venue for each count; 3237(a) permits it only where the offense was begun, continued or completed in the district.
